chapters.core_summary: This introductory chapter explores the history of human transport—from traditional foot travel and log boats to modern high-speed trains and vehicles—to develop a foundational mastery of 5-digit numbers up to 99,999 within the Indian place value system. Students analyze distance logs, odometer readings, and travel budgets, learning to compose, decompose, compare, and round 5-digit numbers to estimate trip costs and journey durations.
key_concepts: Historical evolution of transportation modes as a context for scaling numerical magnitude
Structure of 5-digit numbers using Ten Thousands (TTh), Thousands (Th), Hundreds (H), Tens (T), and Ones (O)
Digit permutation and its impact on relative number magnitude
Odometer reading delta calculations for net distance tracking
Rounding off strategy for rapid estimation of fuel expenses and travel budgets

key_terms.definition: An instrument on a vehicle that measures and displays the total distance traveled in kilometres.
The place value position immediately to the left of Thousands, representing groups of 10,000.
Rearranging the order of digits in a number to form the greatest or smallest possible value.
A reference number (such as the nearest 10, 100, or 1,000) used to simplify numbers for rapid estimation.
The mathematical difference between final and initial odometer readings indicating net travel.

key_takeaways: Place value position determines a digit's contribution to total number magnitude regardless of its face value.
Rounding numbers to the nearest hundred or thousand provides instantaneous estimations for travel planning.
Odometer distance logs use subtraction of 5-digit numbers to determine net kilometres covered.

chapters.core_summary: Through the context of sharing parathas, pizzas, and fruits, this chapter establishes a deep conceptual understanding of fractions as equal parts of a whole or a collection. It emphasizes the Same Whole Rule for valid fraction comparisons, demonstrates how to construct and use fraction strip kits for visual equivalence, and introduces improper fractions and mixed numbers for quantities exceeding one whole.
key_concepts: The Same Whole Rule: fractions can only be compared or combined if derived from equal-sized wholes
Partitioning continuous wholes vs discrete collections into equal fractional groups
Fraction strip construction and visual alignment for discovering equivalent fractions
Representation of quantities greater than 1 using improper fractions and mixed numbers
Equal sharing algorithms for dividing non-divisible whole items among child groups

key_terms.definition: The principle that fractional parts can only be compared or evaluated if they originate from identical whole sizes.
The mathematical act of dividing a continuous object or collection into equal-sized parts.
A set of individual, countable items (like marbles or apples) treated as a unified whole for fractional division.
A set of paper strips folded into halves, quarters, eighths, etc., used for hands-on equivalence exploration.
Expressing a quantity greater than one whole as a combination of a whole number and a proper fraction.

key_takeaways: Fractional size is relative to the size of the whole; half of a small object is less than half of a large object.
Equivalent fractions represent identical amounts through different numerator-denominator ratios.
Sharing $N$ items equally among $M$ people results in a fractional portion of $N/M$ per person.

chapters.core_summary: This chapter introduces geometric angles as measures of rotational turns using interactive tools like paper fans, clock hands, and compass directions. Students classify turns into acute, right, obtuse, and straight angles, learning that degree of opening is completely independent of arm length, and mapping turns to fractions of a full 360° circle.
key_concepts: Angle as a measure of rotational opening between two rays sharing a common vertex
Arm length invariance: angle magnitude depends solely on the degree of turn, not the length of lines drawn
Clock face angular geometry: 12-hour positions create 30° radial increments per hour mark
Fractional circle turns: 1/4 turn = 90° (Right Angle), 1/2 turn = 180° (Straight Angle)
Cardinal compass direction navigation via 90° and 180° clockwise and anti-clockwise pivots

key_terms.definition: The amount of rotation required to turn one arm of an angle to coincide with the other arm.
The property stating that lengthening or shortening the sides of an angle does not alter its angular degree.
Rotational movement following the direction of clock hands (North to East to South to West).
Rotational movement in the direction opposite to clock hands (North to West to South to East).
The constant rotational distance between fixed dial marks, such as 30° between adjacent clock numbers.

key_takeaways: An angle measures the degree of rotation between two intersecting lines, completely unaffected by line length.
A full turn equals 360°, a half turn equals 180° (straight angle), and a quarter turn equals 90° (right angle).
Clocks serve as natural 30° radial tools, where every 5-minute movement of the minute hand represents 30°.

chapters.core_summary: Extending arithmetic operations to large 5-digit logistics problems, this chapter focuses on multi-step addition and subtraction using the column method with regrouping. It incorporates numerical patterns, inverse operations for answer verification, palindromic number generation via the reverse-and-add method, and travel budgeting across multi-city itineraries.
key_concepts: Column-based regrouping across multiple zeroes in 5-digit subtraction
Verification of arithmetic accuracy using the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction
Palindromic number generation through the iterative reverse-and-add algorithm
Consecutive natural number sum patterns and structural number line symmetries
Multi-city travel logistics, fuel budget balancing, and round-trip distance accumulation

key_terms.definition: The sequential borrowing process across multiple consecutive zero digits in subtraction.
Checking a subtraction result by adding the difference to the subtrahend to confirm it equals the minuend.
A number that remains unchanged when its digits are reversed (e.g., 121 or 4,554).
A numerical algorithm where a number is added to its reverse to generate a palindromic sum.
The exact quantitative relationship where minuend equals subtrahend plus difference.

key_takeaways: Subtraction across multiple zeroes requires a cascading regrouping strategy starting from the highest non-zero place value.
Addition and subtraction are inverse operations that serve as self-checking mechanisms in problem solving.
Reversing digits and adding iteratively transforms asymmetric numbers into symmetric palindromic numbers.

chapters.core_summary: This chapter builds comprehensive metric measurement fluency across millimetres, centimetres, metres, and kilometres. Students learn to choose appropriate measurement tools based on object scale, perform compound conversions, use double number lines for proportional scale mapping, and translate map scales into actual ground distances.
key_concepts: Metric unit hierarchy and orders of magnitude from micro (mm) to macro (km)
Proportional scale mapping on double number lines for unit conversion visualization
Cartographic map scale ratios translating paper distance (cm) to ground distance (km)
Selection of appropriate measuring tools based on object dimension and required precision
Compound metric operations with carrying and borrowing across unit boundaries

key_terms.definition: A visual model displaying two parallel lines with aligned equivalent values in different units.
The fixed proportional relationship between a measured distance on a map and the actual distance on Earth.
A length expressed using two metric units simultaneously, such as 3 metres 45 centimetres.
Measurements of very small dimensions requiring millimetre precision, such as coin thickness or seed growth.
Geographical distances requiring kilometre units, such as highway routes between cities.

key_takeaways: Metric conversion relies on fixed base-10 multiples: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1,000 m = 1 km.
Double number lines help visualize proportional equivalence when converting between smaller and larger metric units.
Map scales allow massive geographical distances to be accurately mapped and measured on paper.

chapters.core_summary: Centered around dairy production and agricultural math, this chapter develops flexible mental and written multiplication techniques. Students master place-value zero appending shortcuts, halving and doubling strategies, grid area decomposition for partial products, and the distributive property to solve multi-tier revenue and yield problems.
key_concepts: Place-value zero appending shortcuts when multiplying by multiples of 10, 100, and 1,000
Halving and doubling compensation strategy for mental multiplication simplification
Grid area model for decomposing 2-digit factors into tens and ones partial products
Application of the Distributive Law: $a \times (b + c) = (a \times b) + (a \times c)$
Multi-tier agricultural production modeling: herd size $\rightarrow$ daily yield $\rightarrow$ pricing $\rightarrow$ monthly revenue

key_terms.definition: A grid layout where decomposed factors are multiplied individually before summing to get the total product.
Simplifying multiplication by halving one factor while doubling the other, keeping the product constant.
Breaking a large multiplication problem into smaller sub-arrays that are multiplied separately and added together.
Multiplying the non-zero digits first and appending the total count of trailing zeroes to the product.
Calculating total output by multiplying per-unit production capacity by total unit count.

key_takeaways: Multiplying numbers ending in zero involves multiplying non-zero digits and appending the combined number of zeroes.
Decomposing numbers into tens and ones using grid area models makes multi-digit multiplication clear and error-free.
Halving one factor while doubling the other leaves the total product completely unchanged.

chapters.core_summary: This chapter explores geometry and visual patterns through tessellations (tiling), polygon classification, 7-piece tangram puzzles, and 3D solid nets. Students discover why certain shapes tile without gaps while others do not, classify triangles and quadrilaterals by symmetry, and study polyhedral properties using Euler's Polyhedron Formula.
key_concepts: Interior angle constraints in seamless 2D tessellations (tiling without gaps or overlaps)
Classification of triangles (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and quadrilaterals by side/angle properties
Spatial transformation of flat 2D nets into 3D solid polyhedra (cubes, dodecahedrons, icosahedrons)
Euler's Polyhedron Formula establishing boundary invariance: $Faces + Vertices - Edges = 2$
Geometric dissection and re-assembly of shapes using 7-piece traditional tangram sets

key_terms.definition: An empty space left on a plane when shapes whose interior angles do not divide 360° are placed together.
A flat two-dimensional pattern of joined polygons that can be folded along edges to form a 3D solid.
The invariant topological relation $F + V - E = 2$ holding true for all simple 3D polyhedra.
Cutting a geometric figure into pieces that can be rearranged to form different shapes (e.g., Tangrams).
The structural balance of a closed flat shape based on equal side lengths and interior angle measures.

key_takeaways: Only shapes whose interior angles meet at a point to total exactly 360° can tessellate without leaving gaps.
3D solid shapes can be created by folding specific 2D flat patterns called nets.
For all convex 3D solids, the number of Faces plus Vertices minus Edges always equals 2.

chapters.core_summary: Focusing on mass and liquid volume metrics, this chapter equips students to measure, compare, and convert units from milligrams to tonnes and millilitres to litres. It uses pan balance equilibrium to model algebraic equality, double number lines for proportional fractional mass mapping, and practical scenarios like baking recipes and agricultural shipments.
key_concepts: Mass measurement spectrum: micro-doses (mg), kitchen ingredients (g), body weight (kg), and bulk harvest (Quintals/Tonnes)
Liquid volume measurement scale: medicine doses (ml) to storage tanks (litres)
Pan balance equilibrium as a physical representation of mathematical equation balance
Fractional metric conversions ($1/2 \text{ kg} = 500 \text{ g}$, $3/4 \text{ litre} = 750 \text{ ml}$)
Double number line proportional mapping for converting between metric weight and capacity units

key_terms.definition: The state when both pans of a balance scale hold equal mass, causing the balance indicator to point straight up.
A metric unit of mass equal to 100 kilograms, commonly used for agricultural grain trading.
A metric unit of mass equal to 1,000 kilograms (or 10 Quintals), used for heavy cargo.
Mass measured in milligrams (1/1,000 of a gram), typically used in pharmaceutical active ingredients.
Expressing metric weights as common fractions of a kilogram or gram (e.g., 250 g = 1/4 kg).

key_takeaways: Metric mass conversions rely on thousands: $1,000 \text{ mg} = 1 \text{ g}$, $1,000 \text{ g} = 1 \text{ kg}$, $1,000 \text{ kg} = 1 \text{ Tonne}$.
Pan balance equilibrium demonstrates that adding or removing equal mass keeps both sides balanced.
Fractional parts of a kilogram or litre convert directly to whole sub-units ($1/4 \text{ l} = 250 \text{ ml}$).

chapters.core_summary: Using a coconut harvesting narrative, this chapter teaches division as grouping and fair sharing through algorithm progression. Students explore partial quotients subtraction chunks, zero placement in intermediate quotient steps, the Fundamental Division Identity, and real-world remainder interpretation in packaging and profit sharing.
key_concepts: Fundamental Division Identity: $\text{Dividend} = (\text{Divisor} \times \text{Quotient}) + \text{Remainder}$
Strict Remainder Constraint: the remainder must always be non-negative and strictly less than the divisor ($0 \le R < \text{Divisor}$)
Partial Quotients Method breaking long division into easy subtraction chunks (10s, 20s, 50s)
Explicit zero-placement in quotients when dividend digits are smaller than the divisor
Contextual remainder interpretation: truncating, rounding up, or keeping remainder as fractional leftover

key_terms.definition: A division strategy where friendly multiples of the divisor are repeatedly subtracted from the dividend.
The mathematical rule specifying that a remainder can never be equal to or greater than the divisor.
Inserting a zero in the quotient when an brought-down digit cannot be divided by the divisor.
The equation used to verify division accuracy: $\text{Dividend} = (\text{Divisor} \times \text{Quotient}) + \text{Remainder}$.
The quantity left over after forming maximum equal groups, requiring contextual handling.

key_takeaways: Division calculates either the number of equal groups formed or the size of each equal group.
The remainder must always be strictly smaller than the divisor; otherwise, another equal group can be formed.
Partial quotients allow long division to be completed smoothly using friendly mental multiplication steps.

chapters.core_summary: This chapter explores two-dimensional balance through reflection (line) symmetry and rotational symmetry. Students fold paper figures, examine capital letters and regular polygons for axes of symmetry, build paper firki windmills to observe rotational order, and analyze traditional Rajasthani block printing motifs.
key_concepts: Reflection (Line) Symmetry: an axis that divides a shape into two identical folding mirror halves
Rotational Symmetry: a figure matching its original position when rotated by an angle less than 360°
Order of Rotational Symmetry: the count of matching orientations during one full 360° turn
Symmetrical Independence: shapes can possess rotational symmetry without having line symmetry (e.g., letter Z)
Artistic application of reflection and rotation in traditional block printing and textile patterns

key_terms.definition: An imaginary line along which a figure can be folded so that its two halves match perfectly.
The property of a design appearing completely unchanged after undergoing a partial rotation.
The total number of times a shape coincides with its starting outline during a complete 360° revolution.
The 1/4 turn (90°) rotational symmetry demonstrated by a four-blade paper windmill toy.
Physically folding a cutout shape along a line to verify whether both sides overlap perfectly.

key_takeaways: Line symmetry involves folding mirror halves, whereas rotational symmetry involves partial turning about a center point.
A regular polygon with $N$ sides possesses exactly $N$ lines of symmetry and an order $N$ rotational symmetry.
Some figures (like letters Z, S, N) have rotational symmetry even though they have no lines of reflection symmetry.

chapters.core_summary: centered around quilt patchwork and surface layout, this chapter establishes the distinction between perimeter (1D boundary length) and area (2D enclosed region). Students progress from counting full, half, and partial grid squares to applying length $\times$ breadth formulas, discovering area optimization principles along the way.
key_concepts: Perimeter as 1D total boundary length vs Area as 2D enclosed surface extent
Grid square aggregation rules: full squares = 1, half squares = 0.5, less-than-half = 0, greater-than-half = 1
Area-Perimeter Independence: shapes with the same area can have different perimeters, and vice versa
Area Optimization Principle: among all rectangles with a fixed perimeter, a square encloses maximum area
Practical layout calculations: floor tiling counts, quilt patch totals, and lace border requirements

key_terms.definition: The two-dimensional space contained strictly inside the closed boundary of a flat shape (Area).
The total linear distance around the outside edge of a closed geometric figure (Perimeter).
Designing a rectangle to maximize enclosed surface area for a given perimeter length (achieved by a square).
A standard 1 cm $\times$ 1 cm square used on grid paper to measure area in square centimetres.
Combining two half-covered grid squares to count as one full unit square of area.

key_takeaways: Perimeter measures linear boundary length in units like cm or m; area measures surface region in square units like sq cm or sq m.
A square shape encloses the largest possible area for any given perimeter length.
Shapes with identical areas can have completely different perimeter lengths.

chapters.core_summary: This chapter develops precise temporal awareness by studying time measurement from seconds to hours. Students master the base-60 sexagesimal system, perform duration calculations with hour-minute regrouping, translate between 12-hour AM/PM and 24-hour railway clock formats, and analyze athletic sprint times using digital stopwatches.
key_concepts: Base-60 Sexagesimal System: time units scale by multiples of 60 ($60 \text{ sec} = 1 \text{ min}$, $60 \text{ min} = 1 \text{ hr}$)
High-precision athletic split-second timing using digital stopwatches (hundredths of a second)
Elapsed time span calculation using start time, end time, and base-60 regrouping
Conversion between 12-hour AM/PM clock format and 24-hour transit/railway time
Daily schedule modeling, routine timing, and timetable reading

key_terms.definition: A numeral system using 60 as its base, used globally for measuring time (seconds and minutes).
The total duration that passes between the start and end of an event.
A time convention where the day runs from 00:00 (midnight) to 23:59, avoiding AM/PM markers.
Measuring time intervals smaller than one second, typically in hundredths of a second for sports timing.
Converting 60 accumulated seconds into 1 minute, or 60 accumulated minutes into 1 hour during addition.

key_takeaways: Time arithmetic uses a base-60 system where regrouping occurs at 60 rather than at 10 or 100.
The 24-hour clock format eliminates morning/evening confusion by counting hours continuously from 00:00 to 24:00.
Elapsed time is calculated by subtracting start time from finish time, regrouping hours to 60 minutes when needed.

chapters.core_summary: Through animal characters leaping along numbered grid paths, this chapter makes factors and multiples tangible. Students discover common multiples as shared landing spots, least common multiples (LCM) as first intersections, factor pairs as rectangular arrays, prime vs. composite number structures, and divisibility rules for 2, 3, 5, and 10.
key_concepts: Multiples as forward leap steps along a number line; common multiples as shared landing spots
Least Common Multiple (LCM) as the smallest positive shared landing step
Factors as exact divisors forming rectangular arrays without remainders
Prime numbers (exactly 2 factors: 1 and self) vs Composite numbers (more than 2 factors)
Divisibility test rules for 2 (even end), 5 (ends in 0/5), 10 (ends in 0), and 3 (digit sum divisible by 3)

key_terms.definition: A number on a grid stepped on by two or more jumping animals, representing a common multiple.
Arranging a set number of dots or tiles into complete rectangular grids to discover all factor pairs.
The property of prime numbers having no divisors other than 1 and the number itself.
A quick test to determine whether a number divides evenly into another without doing full long division.
The smallest non-zero number that is a multiple of two or more given numbers.

key_takeaways: Multiples are products generated by multiplying a number by whole numbers; common multiples are shared products.
Factors are whole numbers that divide a target number completely with zero remainder.
Prime numbers have exactly two factors (1 and itself); the number 1 is neither prime nor composite.

chapters.core_summary: Focusing on spatial literacy and navigation, this chapter teaches cardinal directions, map scale reductions, grid coordinate pairs $(x,y)$, and taxicab distance. Students read school floor plans, city maps, and the Delhi Metro network, using map keys and coordinates to trace routes and describe precise locations.
key_concepts: Cardinal orientation (North, South, East, West) using sun position and magnetic compasses
Grid coordinate system $(x,y)$ defining two-dimensional locations via horizontal column ($x$) and vertical row ($y$)
Taxicab grid distance calculating real movement along street grid lines rather than diagonal air lines
Map scale reduction ratio translating paper measurement (cm) to real ground distance (km)
Decoding cartographic legends and tracing transit network routes (e.g., Delhi Metro lines)

key_terms.definition: An ordered pair of numbers $(x, y)$ that pinpoints a precise position on a grid system.
The distance between two points measured strictly along vertical and horizontal grid segments.
A explanatory key on a map defining the meanings of colors, lines, icons, and symbols.
The starting intersection $(0,0)$ on a coordinate grid where horizontal and vertical baseline axes meet.
The constant factor used to shrink real-world distances down to fit onto map paper.

key_takeaways: Coordinate pairs $(x,y)$ uniquely define locations on a grid, where $x$ is horizontal and $y$ is vertical.
Taxicab distance measures path length along grid lines, whereas straight-line distance cuts diagonally.
Map legends and scale ratios allow real-world geography and transit systems to be read and navigated accurately.

chapters.core_summary: This final chapter introduces data handling, organization, and visual analytics. Students collect primary observational data, organize raw counts into 5-stroke tally mark bundles, construct pictographs with scaled icon keys, and draw bar graphs to compare categorical frequencies and identify modes.
key_concepts: Primary data collection via direct counting, measurement, and observational tallying
Tally mark 5-bundle convention (4 vertical strokes crossed by 1 diagonal 5th stroke)
Scaled pictograph representation where 1 icon represents a fixed multiple of data items
Bar graph construction: category X-axis, scaled frequency Y-axis, and bar height proportionality
Data analytics: finding total counts, comparing category differences, and identifying the mode

key_terms.definition: A standard visual grouping of 5 tally marks (卌) that simplifies counting large sets of raw data.
A legend statement defining the exact quantity represented by a single picture icon in a pictograph.
The calibrated numerical scale along a bar graph's Y-axis measuring category quantities.
The data category that occurs with the highest frequency in a data set.
Firsthand gathering of information directly through observation, measurement, or survey counting.

key_takeaways: Grouping tally marks into 5-stroke bundles makes raw data counting fast and error-free.
Pictograph keys state how many real items each picture symbol stands for, including half-symbols.
Bar graph heights are directly proportional to category quantities, allowing instant visual comparisons.
